Title: Nvidia heads for US$470 billion two-day wipeout as CEO affair fallout deepens
Article:
BENGALURU: Nvidia shares extended losses on Tuesday, putting the chip giant on track to shed more than US$470 billion in market value over two sessions as concerns mounted over the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
The CEO's relationship with Alice Huang helped facilitate shipments of at least US$7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, The Information reported on Tuesday, citing two people who know her. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related.
Nvidia's board launched an internal investigation on Sunday, and its independent directors on Tuesday said they had retained former acting US Attorney Joon Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the company's investigation.
The FBI is separately examining whether the 63-year-old Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Huang has told employees he was unfaithful to his wife but provided no details about the relationship.
President Donald Trump said on Monday he had spoken with Huang and asked whether he knew the woman was allegedly a Chinese spy. Trump said Huang told him he had "absolutely no idea" and that he believed the Nvidia CEO.
Trump also said he had not known about the alleged ties when Huang accompanied him to China in May.
However, the New York Times reported on Tuesday that Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio had briefed Trump aboard Air Force One en route to China about US intelligence indicating Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
The briefing marked at least the second time in seven months that Trump had been told about the intelligence, the NYT reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter.
The allegations have intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's governance, export-control compliance and reliance on Huang's leadership, adding to investor unease over whether massive spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure will deliver adequate returns.
Nvidia's shares fell more than 6 per cent following a 4.3 per cent drop on Monday, allowing Microsoft to briefly overtake the AI bellwether as the world's second-most valuable company for the first time since June 2025.
"The investment debate is whether this remains company-specific or triggers restrictions and disruption across AI infrastructure," Bank of America analysts wrote in a note. "We would not equate allegations with proven business damage."
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, along with her husband and sister, built a network of companies across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, The Information reported.
The US Department of Commerce and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Alibaba, Tencent, Megaspeed and Shanghai Century Litong were not immediately available for comment outside regular business hours. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Loke challenges BN MPs to quit cabinet over criticism of Anwar
Article:
MELAKA: DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke has challenged Barisan Nasional members of Parliament to resign from the cabinet instead of continuing to criticise the prime minister and the unity government while remaining in power.
In his first public appearance after stepping down as transport minister, Loke said those who disagreed with Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's leadership should uphold the principle of collective responsibility by relinquishing their cabinet positions.
"If you are not happy, then leave. If you disagree with the prime minister, resign. I have done so. What about you, my friend?" Loke said during a ceramah here last night.
"Every day, you voice your disagreement, while your party attacks the Prime Minister day and night, claiming that one thing or another is wrong. Yet, you remain in the government.
"Every Wednesday and Friday, you attend cabinet meetings chaired by Anwar Ibrahim. What is this all about?" he added.
Loke also questioned why those dissatisfied with the government's policies and allocation decisions continued to remain in the administration instead of leaving.
"There are parties that are dissatisfied and criticise the government every day, questioning why certain ministries are not receiving allocations and raising other issues. Why are they still in the government? Why have they not left?" he said.
The Seremban member of Parliament also urged voters in Melaka to use their ballots in the state election to send a strong message to those pressuring Anwar to dissolve Parliament and pave the way for a general election.
"Although certain quarters are putting pressure on the prime minister to dissolve Parliament, we want to remind them that the mandate remains in Anwar's hands.
"If you are unhappy, you can leave.
"Even though I have resigned as a minister, I have pledged that all DAP MPs will continue to support Anwar. He will remain as Prime Minister," he said.
Although Loke did not mention anyone by name, his
remarks appeared to be directed
at BN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
It was previously reported that Zahid had said it would be better to dissolve Parliament and return the mandate to the people rather than reshuffle the cabinet.
The BN chairman, however, said he saw no need for a cabinet reshuffle at the moment.
Loke had earlier
stepped down as transport minister with immediate effect
following the Kuala Lumpur High Court's decision allowing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest.
He said his resignation was in line with the principled stance he had previously announced.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: ‘Whether or not we accept it, we can vote’: Loke tells Melaka to use ballot box to convey feelings on Najib’s house arrest
Article:
MELAKA, Nov 11 — Fresh from resigning from the federal Cabinet, DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke has urged voters in Melaka who are aggrieved by former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s house arrest to channel their dissatisfaction through the ballot box in Saturday’s state election.
Addressing a Pakatan Harapan ceramah in Ayer Keroh last night, Loke acknowledged widespread public indignation over the decision, while noting that the royal prerogative of mercy enshrined in the Federal Constitution must be respected.
“I am sure many people cannot accept the fact that Najib can serve his sentence under house arrest. Of course, we respect the power of the king, the Federal Constitution and the rule of law. The pardon is provided for under the constitution.
“Whether or not we accept that decision, we can express our views through the ballot box,” he said in a report by
FMT
.
Loke’s rallying call follows his formal resignation as transport minister yesterday, stepping down with immediate effect after the High Court allowed Najib to serve the remainder of his SRC International prison sentence under house arrest.
While acknowledging the national political fallout, Loke cautioned voters against viewing the state polls through a single topic, arguing that the election ultimately decides community representation, regional development, and household welfare.
“Of course, the election is not just about one person. It’s not just about Najib. It’s also about elected representatives and local development,” he said.
Reassuring supporters, Loke reaffirmed that despite his departure from the Cabinet, DAP will continue to deliver its full parliamentary backing to Anwar, guaranteeing government stability until the federal administration completes its full mandate.

Title: Semporna resort had no licence, no expat approval and seven Chinese ‘tourists’ on staff
Article:
TAWAU, Nov 11 — Seven male tourists from China were arrested for allegedly misusing their Social Visit Passes to work at a tourist resort suspected operating illegally in Semporna.
They were among 32 foreigners detained during a two-day Sabah Immigration Department operation in Tawau and Semporna, which began on Sunday.
Sabah Immigration Department Director Datuk Sh Sitti Saleha Habib Yussof said her team inspected six premises and 324 individuals during the operation.
The seven were arrested at a tourist resort for allegedly breaching the conditions of their Social Visit Passes by working there. An eighth detainee, a Filipino man, was arrested at a market.
Nine Chinese nationals and five locals were initially checked at the resort.
Further investigations found that the premises had no expatriate application, was rented on a 4.4-acre plot and did not have a Semporna District Council licence or a tourism operating licence.
“The inspections in Tawau on Sunday involved 159 locals, 42 Indonesians and 17 Filipinos.
“Twenty-four foreigners, comprising 14 Indonesians and 10 Filipinos, were detained in Tawau,” she said, Tuesday.
She said inspections involving 106 individuals in Semporna on Monday resulted in the arrest of another eight foreigners.
She said the team also inspected a construction company with six expatriate workers at Batu 1, 1.5 Jalan Bubul.
However, checks found that all six workers had valid pass extensions and complied with the requirements for the second phase of a commercial development project.
All those detained were investigated under the Immigration Act 1959/63 and taken to the Tawau Immigration Office for further action.
“We remind all employers to comply with the procedures for hiring foreign workers and ensure that their workers’ documents, particularly approvals from the relevant authorities, are valid and registered,” she said.
The two-day operation, led by Saleha, involved 60 immigration officers in Tawau and 42 in Semporna, including senior officers from the state and district levels. — Daily Express

Title: A glowing thing in the sky at 4.40am? Kunak is asking what it was
Article:
KUNAK, Nov 11 — A glowing object was spotted moving across the district’s skies at 4.40am on Monday.
The phenomenon was recorded by a fisherman who happened to be aboard a fishing boat at sea when the object was seen moving across the sky.
The footage raised questions about the object’s identity and origin, including whether it could be linked to a particular atmospheric phenomenon.
So far, there have been no official reports or clear indications from any aerospace agency or relevant authorities on the identity of the object.
The footage was also shared by netizens on Facebook. — Daily Express

Title: Anthony Loke quits Cabinet but says DAP still has Anwar’s back
Article:
MELAKA, Nov 11 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim should not bow to political pressure to dissolve Parliament ahead of schedule.
DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke said the power and prerogative to advise the Yang di-Pertuan Agong on the dissolution of Parliament rested solely with the prime minister.
“We know they are trying to capitalise on the current momentum to pressure the prime minister into dissolving Parliament.
“But I am confident the prime minister will not bow to pressure because he still has the mandate and sufficient support in Parliament to continue his administration.
“He still has another year left in his mandate,” he told reporters after attending a Pakatan Harapan (PH) ceramah in Batu Berendam here last night.
He was responding to calls for Parliament to be dissolved rather than for a Cabinet reshuffle to be carried out, following the impending expiry of Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan’s term as a senator on December 11.
Loke also announced his resignation as Transport Minister with immediate effect yesterday, following the Kuala Lumpur High Court’s decision ordering former Prime Minister Datuk Seri Najib Tun Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence in the SRC International Sdn Bhd case under house arrest at his residence.
He said that despite stepping down from the Cabinet, DAP would continue to give its full support to Anwar to lead the country until the end of the government’s term.
Loke described the calls for Parliament’s dissolution as mere “political games” and advised government allies who no longer shared the same position to make their own decisions.
“If they feel they can no longer work together or no longer respect the prime minister, they can decide whether to continue supporting him or withdraw their support.
“But there is no need to pressure the prime minister to dissolve Parliament,” he said. — Bernama

Title: Old EV batteries could power rural clinics and villages, Nga Kor Ming tells COP31
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — Malaysia has proposed repurposing retired electric vehicle (EV) batteries into energy storage systems to provide a reliable electricity supply to rural communities, indigenous settlements and healthcare facilities, ensuring that the benefits of the circular economy also reach underserved communities.
Housing and Local Government Minister Nga Kor Ming said the proposal, known as the “Circular Equity Dividend”, was among three solutions put forward by Malaysia to accelerate urban circularity globally and advance the zero-waste agenda.
Speaking at the Malaysia Pavilion TED Talk session themed “Closing the Loop: Malaysia’s Journey Towards Zero Waste” at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye, he said the initiative aimed to ensure that the benefits of circularity were distributed more equitably, particularly among underserved communities.
“Malaysia’s Circular Economy Blueprint for Solid Waste 2025-2035 sets national targets of achieving a 40 per cent recycling rate and diverting 53 per cent of waste from landfills by 2035, supported by initiatives such as Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), Separation at Source (SAS) and pilot Zero Waste Districts in Kuala Lumpur and Penang.
“In 2024, Malaysia generated 14.5 million tonnes of municipal solid waste, with food waste accounting for 44.5 per cent and plastics 13.2 per cent, while more than RM2 billion is spent annually on waste management,” he said in a statement issued by the ministry.
Nga said the other two proposals focused on positioning cities as “Material Banks” through mandatory Digital Material Passports, which would track the composition, lifecycle, and reuse potential of materials used in industrial products and infrastructure.
The system would enable valuable resources such as lithium and copper to be recovered and reused rather than discarded.
The second proposal involved replacing conventional landfill tipping fees with Performance-Linked Circular Grants and Municipal Transition Bonds, through which local authorities would receive financial incentives based on measurable environmental outcomes, including recycling rates, landfill diversion and methane reduction.
Drawing on Malaysia’s experience with the “Traffic Light System”, which has been implemented across all 156 local authorities, he said performance-based financing could encourage local councils to invest in recycling facilities, decentralised biodigesters, composting, and other sustainable waste management solutions.
Apart from the TED Talk session, Nga, who is also president of the UN-Habitat Assembly, is scheduled to participate in two panel discussions, namely “Future Fit Cities: Nature, Resilience and Innovation: Shaping the Cities of Tomorrow” and “Zero Waste: From Waste to Watts: Steps to Scale Zero Waste for Climate-Resilient Cities and Energy Security”.
He is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with international counterparts and strategic partners to strengthen cooperation in sustainable urban development and the circular economy.
Taking place from November 9 to 20, COP31 brings together world leaders, ministers, senior government representatives, intergovernmental and multilateral organisations, civil society groups, climate adaptation practitioners, and youth advocates to advance global cooperation on climate action. — Bernama

Title: Perak police seize 48 bitcoin mining machines in Seri Iskandar power theft raid
Article:
IPOH, Nov 11 — A total of 48 units of cryptocurrency (bitcoin) mining machines were seized by the police in an operation yesterday at a residential premises in the Seri Iskandar area, which is believed to be the location for the mining activities with illegal electrical wire connections.
Perak Tengah district police chief Supt Hafezul Helmi Hamzah said the raid was conducted by the Criminal Investigation Division of the Perak Tengah district police headquarters (IPD) in collaboration with the Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) engineering team.
“In addition, two units of fast ethernet switches, one Internet router unit, and one cut electrical cable roll were also seized.
“The case is being investigated under Section 427 of the Penal Code and Section 31(1) of the Electricity Supply Act 1990,” he said in a statement last night.
He said the police take the illegal connection of electricity supply for cryptocurrency mining seriously because such actions are against the law, cause losses to utility providers, and increase the risk of fire and public safety.
Therefore, he advised the public not to engage in any illegal activities and requested that any information related to suspected cryptocurrency mining activities involving electricity theft be reported to the police for further action. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: Supt is short for Superintendent and IPD means Ibu Pejabat Polis Daerah in Malay.

Title: In Dewan Rakyat today: Social media age verification, travel bans over tax, and solar schemes in focus
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — The enforcement status of social media age verification and restrictions on overseas travel were among the issues in focus at the Dewan Rakyat today.
According to the Order Paper published on the Parliament’s official website, Wong Shu Qi (PH-Kluang) will ask the Communications Minister about the enforcement status of social media age verification since June 1, as well as action against platforms that had yet to implement the verification process and the status of the six-month transition period, during the question-and-answer session.
Chow Yu Hui (PH-Raub) will ask the Finance Minister whether the Inland Revenue Board has the authority to restrict overseas travel over outstanding instalments under the CP500 tax instalment payment notice.
He also will seek clarification on when the practice was introduced, how many individuals had been barred from travelling, the legal basis for the restrictions, and whether imposing such restrictions based on estimated taxes that had yet to be finalised was lawful and reasonable.
Meanwhile, Datuk Mohd Isam Mohd Isa (BN-Tampin) will ask the Energy Transition and Water Transformation Minister about the latest achievements of the Solar ATAP and SuRIA Home programmes, including the number of households that had participated, as well as the ministry’s measures to widen access for the B40 and M40 groups through rebates, rental schemes or easy financing options that do not require high upfront costs.
After the question-and-answer session, the Dewan Rakyat will proceed with debates and ministerial replies on the Supply Bill (Budget) 2027 and the 2027 Development Expenditure Estimates Motion at the committee stage.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting is scheduled to run for 37 days until December 8. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: Solar ATAP stands for the Solar Accelerated Transition Action Programme, SuRIA is short for Sustainable Renewable Intended for All, while B40 means the bottom 40 per cent of households by income, and M40 is the middle 40 per cent of households by income.

Title: More boots on the ground: Kelantan Fire Dept weighs 24- or 48-hour duty shifts during monsoon season
Article:
KOTA BHARU, Nov 11 — The Kelantan Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM) is considering extending the duty shifts of its personnel to up to 48 hours in the event of major flooding during the 2026/2027 Northeast Monsoon (MTL), to strengthen its rescue operation capabilities.
Its director, Farhan Sufyan Borhan, said the measure could involve adjustments to the current shift system, from 12-hour rotations to 24- or 48-hour shifts, depending on operational requirements and the situation on the ground during a disaster.
He explained that personnel currently work in three teams on a 12-hour shift system to ensure fire station operations continue around the clock.
“To increase the number of personnel available during major floods, we will manage leave and switch from 12-hour to 24-hour shifts, thereby increasing the number of personnel on duty,” he told Bernama recently.
He added that a freeze on leave could also be imposed, depending on the severity of the disaster, to ensure sufficient manpower, particularly when rescue operations require the deployment of more personnel.
However, Farhan Sufyan stressed that the availability of assets, including boats, trucks and four-wheel-drive vehicles, was equally important to operational effectiveness, as increasing manpower alone would not be sufficient without the necessary equipment.
In a related development, Kelantan JBPM has identified vulnerable groups, including the elderly, persons with disabilities (PwDs) and bedridden patients living in flood-prone areas, to facilitate evacuation efforts in the event of flooding.
He said the exercise was carried out in coordination with the State Disaster Management Committee, involving the Social Welfare Department (JKM) and the Health Department.
He added that information on residents requiring special assistance during evacuation, including the number of elderly people and persons with disabilities in high-risk areas, had been compiled to support operational planning.
“We have identified the number of PwDs and elderly people in these areas who require attention, and the matter has been coordinated at the State Disaster Management Committee level,” he said.
He said the actual evacuation process would depend on prevailing conditions when a disaster occurred, particularly during its initial stages, which were usually challenging for rescue agencies.
He added that training and inter-agency cooperation were also crucial to ensuring the safe and orderly evacuation of vulnerable groups.
Last Sunday, the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) issued a caution-level warning for continuous rain in several areas in Kelantan, Pahang and Sabah, as well as throughout Terengganu, effective until today.
MetMalaysia said the affected areas in Kelantan included Tanah Merah, Pasir Mas, Tumpat, Kota Bharu, Machang, Bachok, Pasir Puteh, Kuala Krai and Jeli.
Following the warning, the National Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre under the Department of Irrigation and Drainage indicated that nine districts in Kelantan could potentially experience flooding during the same period. — Bernama
*Editor’s note: JBPM stands for Jabatan Bomba dan Penyelamat Malaysia in Malay, MTL is short for Monsun Timur Laut (Northeast Monsoon), and JKM is Jabatan Kebajikan Masyarakat (Social Welfare Department).

Title: ECRL, bus, plane or car? Weighing the cost, time and convenience of getting to the East Coast
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — For travellers heading to the East Coast, the options may soon extend beyond the familiar bus, plane or car, with the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) set to offer another way to get there.
But choosing how to travel may depend on more than just the ticket price, as the ECRL, buses, flights and driving each come with different trade-offs in journey time, convenience and overall door-to-door costs.
With ECRL passenger services set to begin on December 12, the question is which mode of transport offers the best value once ticket prices, fuel, tolls, parking and transfers are factored in.
What the numbers say
The ECRL’s 523km Gombak-Kota Bharu route provides a basis for comparing the available travel options.
One-way Economy fares start at RM125 per person for Transit services and RM147 for Express services.
However, fares may vary depending on travel time, demand and seat availability. Discounts are available for students, children aged two to 12, Malaysians aged 60 and above, persons with disabilities and government pensioners.
Express trains are expected to take about four hours, stopping at four main stations, compared with up to five hours for Transit services, which stop at all 16 scheduled stations.
Conventional express buses remain cheaper, with one-way fares from Kuala Lumpur to Kota Bharu ranging from RM44 to RM68. However, the journey takes about nine hours and 30 minutes under ideal traffic conditions.
Flying offers the fastest journey, with direct flights from Kuala Lumpur to Kota Bharu taking about an hour and 10 minutes. One-way fares range from RM123 to RM167, comparable with ECRL tickets.
For motorists, using subsidised Budi95 petrol at RM1.99 per litre and an illustrative fuel consumption rate of 4.5 litres per 100km for a Perodua Myvi 1.3L, the estimated one-way cost of driving about 420km from Gombak to Kota Bharu is RM37.60 for petrol and RM17 in tolls.
This brings the estimated one-way cost to RM54.60, excluding parking and other incidental expenses, for a journey of about six hours and 25 minutes under ideal traffic conditions.
A new train, a new choice
For 24-year-old journalist Wong Ci En, the ECRL offers another travel option for trips back to her hometown of Chukai, Terengganu, where convenience and journey time are key considerations.
Wong said she usually takes an express bus when travelling alone or hitches a ride with a family member, with the journey by road taking between four and five hours.
“One-way express bus tickets from Terminal Bersepadu Selatan to Chukai cost almost RM50, while an ECRL ticket from Terminal Bersepadu Gombak (TBG) to Chukai costs RM69.
“I will definitely consider using ECRL because it is fast, has no traffic congestion and saves a lot of time,” she said, noting that the estimated journey time on the ECRL was less than three hours.
Still, Wong said the distance between her current home in Seri Kembangan, Selangor, and TBG could deter her from taking the ECRL.
However, she said she would seriously consider the service if the inconvenience of last-mile travel could be addressed.
For 31-year-old pharmacist See Hui Qi, who travels frequently between Kuantan, Pahang, and Kuala Lumpur, the ECRL offers another option, with convenience, journey time and affordable fares influencing her choice.
She currently prefers driving or taking the bus from Kuantan to Kuala Lumpur to visit her siblings or catch flights from KLIA.
“Yes, I might consider taking the ECRL, especially during festive seasons when traffic congestion is common.
“Since I live in Petaling Jaya, connecting to the Kelana Jaya Line via Gombak station through the TBG interchange would also make it a feasible option for my future trips.
“In terms of the time saved, I think the ECRL ticket prices are reasonable for me,” she said.
Still, she said she would prefer travelling with her family for greater comfort, while prioritising convenience and journey time when travelling alone.
For 55-year-old university lecturer Khairana Sabtu, who travels with her family of five to Kota Bharu, Kelantan, to visit her parents, the ECRL is a timely addition that offers an alternative to road travel.
Although she prefers driving, she recalled being stuck in heavy traffic for almost 23 hours during a Hari Raya trip in 2022.
“I think the ECRL is the best choice for travelling back to Kota Bharu, as the ticket fares are affordable for my family and me, while the shorter journey time is another advantage.
“I just hope the ticket price will remain the same, especially during festive seasons and school holidays,” she said.
Beyond ticket prices, comfort is another key consideration. Khairana said she expected the ECRL to offer a journey as comfortable as that of KTM’s Electric Train Service (ETS), which she had previously taken to Penang and Johor.
Which is the best choice?
Ultimately, the best option depends on the balance travellers are willing to strike between cost, journey time and convenience.
While express buses offer the lowest fares, journey times can exceed 10 hours during peak festive periods because of traffic congestion, with extreme gridlock sometimes stretching trips to as long as 20 hours.
Although buses remain an economical option for budget-conscious travellers, prolonged journeys can be tiring, particularly for those travelling with young children or older family members.
Flights offer the quickest journey, but travellers must factor in additional time for airport transfers and check-in, as well as the cost of getting to the airport. Fares can also fluctuate with demand, potentially increasing travel costs for those booking at short notice or travelling in larger groups.
Driving offers greater flexibility, particularly for families and groups, but the overall expense depends on the vehicle, fuel consumption, driving conditions and route, with other incidental costs adding to the bill.
Journey times can also increase significantly during school holidays and festive seasons, making long drives more exhausting for families travelling with children or older people.
The ECRL offers a faster and potentially more comfortable alternative to road travel, with predictable journey times and less physical fatigue than driving or spending long hours on a bus.
However, fares can add up, especially for large groups and return trips, while passengers are restricted to designated stations and may need additional transport to reach their final destinations.

Title: How much has China influenced Chinese Malaysian youths?
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — China’s growing influence among Chinese Malaysians youths is increasingly visible not only through the products they buy, but also through the entertainment, social media platforms and language trends.
Participants in a recently published IMAN Research study described exposure to Chinese digital platforms and content, including trends, slang and expressions, have spread beyond China through online communities.
The report,
Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness
, examined how such exposure shapes everyday cultural consumption, particularly among young people familiar with Mandarin.
However, the researchers found that consuming Chinese content did not automatically change how participants viewed their national identity.
Some interviewees were more concerned about the wider implications of imported cultural content and the circulation of political messages, while others regarded the material primarily as entertainment or a convenient source of information.
Their views also differed according to how politically engaged they were and how closely they followed developments in China.
The report, based on interviews with 116 Chinese Malaysians youths aged between 18 and 35 across peninsular Malaysia, found that participants held varied views of China’s rise.
Some admired its technological and economic development, while others raised concerns about its regional ambitions, human rights record and implications for Malaysian businesses.
Those who were more politically aware tended to express stronger concerns about sovereignty and China’s regional influence.
For others, the immediate benefits of affordable products, business opportunities and technological progress were more relevant to their everyday lives.
Competition for local businesses
China’s presence was also felt through the products participants bought and the businesses they encountered.
For consumers, platforms such as Taobao offered access to affordable products and a wider range of goods without having to travel to major cities to find them.
The convenience and lower prices made these platforms attractive, with some participants describing their interactions with China as primarily commercial rather than political.
For local businesses, however, the picture was more complicated.
The report found that some participants viewed Chinese companies and products as a source of pressure on Malaysian businesses, particularly those that relied on importing and reselling goods.
The availability of cheaper products through Chinese suppliers and online platforms has reduced the role of local intermediaries, forcing some businesses to reconsider how they operate.
One example involved a local car workshop that shifted away from relying mainly on selling automotive parts and placed greater emphasis on installation and other services.
As customers gained easier access to parts directly from suppliers, the business had to find other ways to remain competitive by offering services that required local expertise.
Other participants viewed the competition more positively.
One business owner described it as a “catfish effect”, arguing that stronger competition from Chinese companies could push Malaysian businesses to improve rather than remain comfortable with existing practices.
The report also noted that Chinese beverage and lifestyle brands had demonstrated that consumers outside major cities could be willing to pay for premium products when the concept and quality were appealing.
Language as a working advantage
The report also examined how knowledge of Mandarin could create opportunities in workplaces dealing with Chinese businesses and investors.
One interviewee, a lawyer, described the preference among some Chinese entities for working with people who speak their language.
“The reality is that Chinese entities coming here prefer dealing with those who speak their language,” the participant said.
However, the report suggests that language alone is not necessarily enough.
The ability to understand Chinese business expectations while navigating Malaysian laws, workplace practices and social contexts can also be valuable.
This places young Chinese Malaysians youths who can bridge the two environments in a position to facilitate communication and business relationships.
China has not displaced local identity
Despite China’s growing presence in their daily lives, the researchers found that participants generally continued to identify with Malaysia.
The report noted that only one respondent placed a transnational Chinese identity above their local identity.
Its findings suggest that young Chinese Malaysians do not necessarily view China through a single cultural or political lens.
Their responses are shaped by how they encounter the country — whether as consumers, workers, entrepreneurs or users of digital platforms.

Title: IMAN Research finds gaps in how Chinese youths understand politics and public institutions
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — A young Chinese individual may know about the latest political controversy, follow debates on social media or have strong views about the rising cost of living.
Yet, he or she could still be unsure which government agency is responsible for addressing a problem in their neighbourhood, or how politics fit into everyday life application.
That gap between following politics and understanding how the system works emerged as one of the findings in a recently published IMAN Research study on Malaysian Chinese youths.
The interviews found that participants often associated national politics with elections, scandals, party manoeuvring and disputes over race and religion.
When discussing issues closer to home, such as housing, education, wages and local services, however, they were often more specific about what was going wrong and what they wanted changed.
The question — is whether young people know how these everyday concerns connect to public institutions, who makes the decisions and where they can turn to have their voices heard.
The report,
Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness
, is based on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 across Peninsular Malaysia.
Civic education that does not stick
One of the report’s findings was that the 116 participants vaguely recall what they had learnt through the former Pendidikan Sivik dan Kewarganegaraan subject or how it had shaped their understanding of politics as adults.
Some remembered civic lessons being replaced by subjects considered more important.
One participant said civic and political education should go beyond memorising Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy or the structure of Parliament.
“We should be learning about how the democratic system works from a young age,” the participant said, adding that students should understand what voting and representation mean and why they matter.
The researchers stressed that exposure to political events was not the same as having the knowledge to interpret them.
Participants could know that a controversy had taken place or feel strongly about an issue without understanding which institution was responsible, what powers an elected representative held or what action citizens could realistically take.
Who shapes their political understanding?
The report introduces what it calls the “First-to-Door” model to explain how young people develop their understanding of politics.
It describes how the first trusted source that makes politics meaningful or understandable can shape how a person interprets information encountered later.
The “first” source does not necessarily mean the earliest one encountered.
Rather, it refers to the person, platform or experience that first provides a convincing framework for understanding political events.
For some participants, that source was family.
The researchers found that political understanding could be shaped by parents who discussed elections, government policies and experiences of exclusion.
However, family influence could also operate through silence.
One participant who voted for the first time recalled being unsure about which party logo to select, despite knowing that voting was expected of her.
She said her family did not discuss politics at home.
Social media was another important source of political information, although participants did not necessarily consume the same discussions.
The report found that language influenced which political conversations reached them, with some participants deliberately following both Chinese- and Malay-language media to avoid missing discussions taking place in different public spheres.
One interviewee said: “If I only consumed Chinese-language media, I would miss entire waves of discourse happening in the Malay public sphere.”
The researchers cautioned, however, that consuming news in multiple languages did not automatically mean someone had a stronger understanding of politics.
Some participants read only headlines, while others compared different commentators and perspectives before forming their own views.
Knowing politics is not the same as being involved
The report also distinguishes between political knowledge and political proximity.
Political knowledge refers to understanding how institutions work, the responsibilities of different office-holders and public issues.
Political proximity, meanwhile, refers to how directly someone encounters political work, actors and decision-making — through activities such as community organising, campaigning, party work or regular contact with elected representatives.
The researchers used a matrix to illustrate how these two dimensions can overlap without necessarily developing together.
For example, someone may become involved in a political party or be invited to assist a representative without fully understanding how government institutions work.
Another person may follow political developments closely and understand public policy, but remain outside political organisations or direct political activity.
The report stressed that the matrix was exploratory, with its four positions illustrating possible combinations rather than fixed categories of Malaysian Chinese youths.
It also found that involvement in political organisations could provide participants with networks, procedural knowledge and confidence, but did not automatically produce independent political judgement.
Similarly, contact with elected representatives could help participants understand how to raise complaints or seek assistance, although it might not necessarily teach them which government agency was responsible for a particular issue.
Making civic participation practical
The researchers recommended strengthening civic education by moving beyond lessons on government structures and electoral procedures towards practical political and media literacy.
Students should be given opportunities to engage with local institutions, conduct community research, understand how public decisions are made and interact with people outside their immediate social circles.
One programme that others could exemplify is by Pay Fong Middle School in Melaka.
The school programme includes visits to local heritage sites, documenting historical places and interviewing residents from different ethnic backgrounds.
The researchers also recommended that state and local authorities establish neighbourhood advisory bodies and support youth-led community projects.
Their broader discussion is that young people should encounter democratic participation as part of everyday life, rather than something limited to voting during elections.
The report noted that practical opportunities to understand and engage with institutions could help young people distinguish political arguments from the processes through which public decisions are made.

Title: Najib arrives at Taman Duta residence to begin his house arrest (VIDEO)
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — Former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak has arrived at his residence in Jalan Langgak Duta here today to begin serving the remainder of his SRC International prison sentence under house arrest.
Najib’s arrival at his Taman Duta home followed a fresh High Court order this afternoon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence at the residence until August 23, 2028.
He arrived at his residence at about 9.25pm in a silver SUV, accompanied by a convoy of several vehicles believed to be carrying security personnel, which escorted him into the compound as reporters waited outside.
A few of his supporters, who had waited here since 5pm, shouted “
Hidup Bossku
” repeatedly as Najib’s vehicle passed by.
Earlier today, High Court judge Datuk Aslam Zainuddin directed the Court Registrar to issue a new warrant of release after hearing submissions from Najib’s lawyers and Deputy Public Prosecutors.
Aslam said the new order cancelled the November 6 order and replaced it with one allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence at home.
A vehicle believed to be carrying former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak arrives at his residence in Jalan Langgak Duta, Kuala Lumpur on November 10, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
The fresh order came after the Attorney-General’s Chambers sought a review of the previous court order, saying clarification was needed over its wording and legal effect.
Najib had remained at Kajang Prison despite an earlier court order paving the way for his house arrest, after the AGC said implementation should be deferred pending legal clarification.
The former prime minister’s conditional royal pardon, granted on September 18, allows him to serve the remainder of his SRC International sentence under house arrest until August 23, 2028, subject to the stipulated conditions.
The arrangement followed the payment of the RM50 million fine imposed on Najib in the SRC International case.
Najib was initially sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment and fined RM210 million in 2020. The Federal Territories Pardons Board reduced his sentence to six years and the fine to RM50 million in January 2024.

Title: Viral video leads to probe into firecracker incident in Klang
Article:
SHAH ALAM, Nov 10 — Police are investigating an incident involving an individual setting off firecrackers at the traffic light junction of Jalan Tengku Kelana, Kawasan 1, Klang, which endangered public safety on Nov 8.
South Klang district police chief ACP Lim Jit Huey said the incident, which occurred at about 1 am, went viral on social media before police received a report regarding the matter.
“Police have opened an investigation paper under Section 286 of the Penal Code for negligent conduct involving explosive substances.
“Those with information are urged to contact the South Klang District Police Headquarters or any nearby police station to assist in the investigation,” he said in a statement today.
Earlier, a video went viral on social media showing an individual setting off firecrackers at the traffic light junction, obstructing the road and disrupting the movement of other road users. — Bernama

Title: ‘I should have stepped down today’: Hannah Yeoh says Anthony Loke paid the price instead
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh said she should have resigned from the Cabinet today, but DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke wanted the party’s ministers to remain in government to fulfil their promises to the people.
“I should have stepped down today, but my Secretary-General wants us to fulfill all our promises to the people and complete the unfinished work. In the end, he paid the price himself,” she said in a Facebook post today.
Her remarks came after Loke announced his resignation as transport minister with immediate effect, following the Kuala Lumpur High Court’s decision allowing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his SRC International prison sentence under house arrest.
Loke had first announced his intention to resign in September following the conditional pardon granted to Najib, but remained in the Cabinet temporarily at Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim’s request.
DAP had decided that its other ministers and deputy ministers would remain in government to maintain political stability and complete outstanding commitments.

Title: ‘Alhamdulillah’: Rosmah welcomes news of Najib’s clearance for house arrest
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — Datin Seri Rosmah Mansor has expressed gratitude following the return of her husband, former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak, to their residence in Jalan Langgak Duta here today after a court order allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house detention.
“Alhamdulillah,” Rosmah said briefly when contacted by
Berita Harian
.
She said she was awaiting Najib’s arrival at their Taman Duta home, where he will serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house detention.
Earlier today, the High Court issued a fresh order allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his reduced six-year prison term under house detention until Aug 23, 2028, with immediate effect.
A survey of the area found the atmosphere outside the residence calm, with security arrangements in place as preparations were made for Najib’s return home.
Najib’s house detention follows recent legal developments concerning the implementation of the remainder of his sentence.

Title: Investigation papers on Penang assemblyman accused of injuring wife still under DPP review
Article:
GEORGE TOWN, Nov 10 — Penang police are awaiting further instructions from the Deputy Public Prosecutor (DPP) on the investigation into an allegation that a state assemblyman injured his wife in an incident on October 31.
Penang Chief Police Officer Datuk Dennis Lim Kwang Keng said the investigation papers were still with the DPP's office for further review.
"The investigation papers are still with the DPP, and police are awaiting further instructions on the case," he told Bernama when contacted tonight for an update on the investigation.
Earlier, police confirmed receiving a report from the assemblyman's wife, who alleged that her husband had injured her at their home here on Oct 31.
Lim was previously reported as saying that police had opened an investigation paper under Section 323 of the Penal Code to investigate the incident. — Bernama

Title: Home Ministry says ready to carry out Najib’s house arrest; court order today cleared the air
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — The Home Ministry this evening said it is prepared to carry out a new court order today for former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to be on house arrest until August 2028.
In his statement on his ministry’s readiness to execute the court’s new order, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the High Court’s latest order has helped answered legal uncertainties surrounding Najib’s house arrest.
He was referring to the High Court in Kuala Lumpur’s decision this afternoon to revoke an earlier November 6 “Order of Discharge on Payment of Fine” and to replace it with a new order that will require Najib to serve his remaining jail term under house arrest until August 23, 2028.
The house arrest will be at Najib’s private residence at No 11, Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta in Kuala Lumpur.
Najib, who was wearing a light blue
baju Melayu
top, was brought from Kajang Prison and was present at the court proceedings this afternoon.
On November 6, Umno had paid the RM50 million fine on behalf of Najib, as this was the condition in the Yang di-Pertuan Agong’s September conditional pardon to allow him to be on house arrest in the SRC International case.
But Najib had remained in Kajang Prison since November 6, as the Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) had highlighted legal uncertainties related to Najib’s house arrest.
Earlier today, the AGC filed an application at the High Court to rectify or correct the earlier court order and also to issue a new court order that would enable the house arrest, which resulted in this afternoon’s court proceedings.
Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail explained that the delay in implementing Najib’s house arrest previously was due to legal issues regarding interpretation of the conditional pardon order and the legal effect of the November 6 “Order of Discharge”, especially regarding the implementation of the remaining sentence via house arrest. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
Saifuddin today said the Home Ministry always respects and upholds the Agong’s royal pardon decision in line with the ruler’s powers under Article 42 of the Federal Constitution, and that all decisions made through constitutional channels should be respected and carried out according to the law.
Saifuddin then explained that the delay in implementing Najib’s house arrest previously was due to legal issues regarding interpretation of the conditional pardon order and the legal effect of the November 6 “Order of Discharge”, especially regarding the implementation of the remaining sentence via house arrest.
“The High Court’s decision today has clarified this issue,” he said in his statement that was titled as the government’s position on the implementation of the royal pardon involving Najib.
He said the Home Ministry respects the AGC’s position that the legal issue required clarification through a court process, adding that this approach is important to ensure each government action has a clear and valid legal basis.
“As Home Minister, I stress that the Ministry’s and the Prisons Department’s responsibility is to ensure that each decision related to the execution of sentence and detention is carried out according to the law and valid court orders,” he said in his statement.
“This case is a high-profile case which has huge political implications and public perception,” he said, urging for everyone to handle this maturely and responsibly without letting political polemics from affecting public confidence in the country’s institution.
Saifuddin concluded by saying that the federal government would continue to defend the Malay rulers’ role and position within the framework of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy, while upholding constitutional supremacy, rule of law and the judiciary’s independence.
“These principles complete each other and are the basis for national stability,” he concluded.
While Najib will be able to serve the rest of his SRC International jail term at home until August 23, 2028, he is also facing a separate 15-year jail term in his other trial involving over RM2 billion of 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) funds.
The High Court in December 2025 had ordered Najib to immediately start serving his 15-year jail term in the 1MDB case after he completes his SRC International jail term.
Najib is currently appealing his 1MDB conviction and jail term, with the Court of Appeal yet to hear his appeal.

Title: How uncertainty over university pathways shapes Chinese youths’ choices
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — For some Malaysian Chinese youths, deciding where to study after secondary school is not simply a matter of choosing a course or university.
Most of these choices are made through weighing how secure they feel about their chances of getting into their preferred programme.
In a research conducted by IMAN Research, they found that uncertainty over public university admissions, differences between pre-university pathways and concerns about access to certain courses had influenced how some the research participants approached their education.
In its recently published report,
Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness
, draws on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 across Peninsular Malaysia.
The study found that education was one of the areas where participants’ perceptions of fairness were particularly shaped by their own experiences, expectations and accounts they had heard from others.
Some participants described choosing private education or overseas study rather than applying through the public university admission system.
One interviewee, for instance, went directly to a private university without applying through the Unit Pusat Universiti (UPU), citing concerns within the family about the chances of securing a place through the public route.
Another participant who wanted to study medicine declined an offer to pursue biotechnology and instead went to China.
The report describes these decisions as examples of how young people may seek alternatives when public pathways appear uncertain.
However, it also makes an important distinction between barriers participants personally experienced, obstacles they anticipated and accounts they had heard from family members or their wider community.
These are not the same kinds of evidence, and the researchers cautioned against treating every disappointing outcome or decision not to apply as proof of discrimination.
Matriculation and UPU are not the same
The research found that there was a recurring source of confusion among participants — the relationship between the matriculation quota and university admissions through UPU.
The report clarifies that the 90 per cent Bumiputera quota applies to entry into matriculation, not to UPU’s university selection formula.
UPU ranks applicants from STPM, matriculation and other equivalent qualifications using 90 per cent academic marks and 10 per cent co-curricular marks.
Candidates are considered according to merit, programme requirements, available places and their course preferences.
The report said the UPU pathway itself does not have an ethnic quota system.
However, the researchers noted that differences between Sijil Tinggi Persekolahan Malaysia (STPM) and matriculation could still raise questions about fairness.
STPM generally takes one and a half years, while the main matriculation programme takes one year.
The two pathways also use different assessment structures.
How are they different?
STPM students may progress through school, zone, district, state and national competitions, while matriculation students compete within a structure centred on inter-college competitions.
Citing figures that showed 16 per cent of matriculation students achieved a cumulative grade point average of 4.0, compared with 3.09 per cent of STPM students, the researchers suggest these differences be examined when considering how students from the two pathways are assessed
For popular courses such as medicine, pharmacy and dentistry at public universities, matriculation students accounted for more than 97 per cent of places in 2023, while STPM students made up less than 3 per cent, according to figures cited in the report.
These figures were used to illustrate differences in outcomes between the pathways, rather than establish that any individual applicant had been unfairly treated.
When students look for alternatives
The report found that family resources played an important role in determining whether young people could pursue alternatives when they felt uncertain about public education pathways.
Some could afford private universities or overseas study, while others had fewer options.
This meant that the ability to work around perceived barriers was not equally available to everyone.
The researchers also noted that concerns inherited from parents or community members could influence decisions even before a student applied for a place.
In such cases, these Chinese youths people might rule out a pathway based on what they had heard about the system, rather than on a direct experience of rejection.
The report recommends that the government make university admissions criteria, selection mechanisms and intake data more transparent and accessible.
It also calls for students to be given clearer information about how different pre-university qualifications are assessed and how they affect university options.
The researchers said differences in co-curricular opportunities between STPM and matriculation should also be reviewed, alongside clearer pathways for students holding the Unified Examination Certificate who wish to enter public universities.
Rather than redesigning the entire pre-university system, the report suggests addressing specific areas where the students face uncertainty or unequal opportunities.
Its broader concern is that when students cannot clearly understand how public education pathways work, they may make decisions based on assumptions, family experiences or perceived limitations — potentially narrowing their choices before they have fully explored them.

Title: Najib’s house arrest: What did the AGC ask the High Court to clarify today?
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — The Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) today sought to ensure that Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s house arrest arrangements explicitly provided for his return to Kajang Prison on August 24, 2028, to serve his separate 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) prison sentence.
In its written application, the prosecution requested that the High Court replace a November 6 discharge order with new terms clarifying Najib’s remaining SRC International sentence and his subsequent imprisonment in the 1MDB case.
The application specified that Najib should “be transferred back to Kajang Prison on August 24, 2028, to serve the sentence imposed on him in the 1MDB case”.
It also sought to specify that his SRC sentence would end on August 23, 2028, with his return to prison subject to any court order then in force.
The prosecution said the 1MDB prison sentence had been directed to begin once his SRC sentence ended, arguing that “the end date of the SRC sentences must be stated with certainty”.
It explained that Najib’s payment of the RM50 million fine on November 6 discharged his liability for the fine and imprisonment for non-payment, but did not extinguish his remaining SRC prison sentence.
The AGC also argued that the earlier discharge order, which used a standard form for release upon payment of a fine, could be interpreted as releasing Najib from his remaining SRC sentence altogether.
Citing provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code governing imprisonment warrants, the prosecution said there was an urgent need for a clear order in accordance with the law.
High Court issues replacement order
High Court judge Datuk Aslam Zainuddin subsequently set aside the November 6 discharge order and issued a replacement order allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his SRC sentence under house arrest until August 23, 2028.
Aslam’s new order only states that it replaces the previous cancelled order and that Najib must remain in house arrest until August 23, 2028; it is silent on other matters including, notably, any requirement for Najib to return to prison past this date to serve a separate sentence from the main 1MDB trial.
At the hearing, Najib’s lead counsel Tan Sri Muhammad Shafee Abdullah had argued that the original discharge order was already clear, as the RM50 million fine required under the conditional royal pardon had been paid.
Speaking to reporters afterwards, Shafee welcomed the court’s clarification despite maintaining that the original order was sound.

Title: Rapid KL confirms brake fault behind smoke incident at KL Sentral (VIDEO)
Article:

In a statement, the rail operator said the incident is believed to have been caused by the train's braking system, which resulted in visible smoke being emitted from the affected train.
