Title: Beyond assumptions: IMAN Research’s journey into the lives of Chinese youths
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — When Violet Lee Zi Yi began researching Malaysian Chinese youths, she admitted she initially approached the community with assumptions about its relative economic advantages, resources and access to opportunities.
What she discovered through interviews with these youths across Peninsular Malaysia was a much more complicated picture.
“I initially thought Chinese is a unitary block. It is so different,” Lee said in an interview about the findings of IMAN Research’s report,
Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness
.
The report, prepared by Lee and co-researcher Liew Liang Hong, is based on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 conducted from August 2025 to April 2026.
It examines Chinese youths on how they understand their identity, navigate opportunities and inequality, and relate to politics and public institutions.
Rather than treating Malaysian Chinese youths as a single political or cultural group, the research found that their experiences were shaped by factors including family history, language, schooling, religion, socioeconomic background and where they grew up.
For some, regional identities such as being Penangite, Johorean or an anak Terengganu were just as important in defining who they were.
“When I started the research, I went into it with a mindset of —
apa lagi Cina mahu
or what else do the Chinese want?
“I wanted to understand what more Malaysian Chinese youths wanted, so I had assumptions about the community’s relative advantages.
“But the interviews changed my perception. Everyone’s experience is so diverse, so different, and every conversation just added what I had never imagined before,” she said.
One example was how family history could shape identity differently across generations.
Lee said she had not initially considered how being a third-generation Malaysian Chinese could produce a different outlook from being fourth-generation, depending on how grandparents and great-grandparents had spoken about China and their family’s history.
She said these differences emerged naturally during the conversations, illustrating how the research uncovered experiences that the team had not anticipated when designing its questions.
Belonging is not always straightforward
The report found that national identity did not necessarily come at the expense of Chinese cultural identity.
Some participants described themselves primarily as Malaysian, while others considered Malaysian Chinese an inseparable identity.
Others placed strong emphasis on their state or hometown.
For some interviewees from the East Coast, being an anak Terengganu was central to how they described home, even as they recognised restrictions associated with being part of a minority community.
One participant described the distinction between feeling at home and feeling politically restricted, saying: “As a layman I feel I belong, but in politics I feel being restricted, like in Matriculation and fund allocation.”
The report said these feelings could coexist: participants could feel emotionally attached to Malaysia while questioning how public resources and institutions treated different communities.
It also found that everyday interactions could foster a sense of shared Malaysian identity.
Participants spoke positively about ordinary experiences such as eating at mamak restaurants, mixing languages and joining one another’s festivals.
However, the researchers cautioned against romanticising these interactions, noting that cordial relationships did not necessarily translate into deeper understanding or erase concerns about institutional fairness.
The cost of pragmatism
One of the report’s central findings is what it calls “self-cornering” — the tendency to find private ways around perceived problems rather than challenge the institutions behind them.
The report found that some young people responded to uncertainty over public opportunities by working harder, relying on family networks, paying for alternatives or looking overseas.
These decisions could be practical and help individuals secure their futures, but the researchers argued that they also carried wider consequences.
When those with sufficient resources could find private alternatives, the institutions and policies behind their concerns remained unchanged. Those without the means to find alternatives could be left with fewer options.
The report also distinguished between inequality personally experienced by participants, barriers they anticipated and accounts they had heard from family or community members.
It cautioned against treating every disappointing outcome as proof of discrimination, while recognising that inherited accounts could influence how young people assessed their prospects.
Wanting to be heard
Another finding concerned the distance between young people and the organisations or institutions expected to represent them.
Lee said she was struck by how some interviewees did not consider their own opinions valuable simply because they were not politically vocal.
“We wanted to include young people who were not already active in community organisations or political circles, rather than relying mainly on those who were accustomed to speaking publicly.
“Only about 10 to 15 per cent of those recruited were young leaders.
“This was important because young people who were already involved in organisations were often more comfortable expressing their views, while others might not see their own experiences as worth sharing,” she said.
The research team also found that established community leaders could say they wanted younger people to participate, yet were sometimes reluctant to give them meaningful space.
Lee said this could leave young people struggling to find where they could contribute, while older leaders continued to hold the resources and decision-making positions.
She also questioned the narrow definition of success within parts of the community, where financial achievement and professional status could be valued more visibly than civic or political participation.
“Chinese youth are not rewarded socially if you are in politics. Only if you become a politician, you become someone famous, then yes, you’re recognised,” she said.
Those working behind the scenes, she added, were less likely to receive recognition.
Lee said the research also found that some young people wanted to move beyond racialised political thinking but were unsure how to do so.
“They are conditioned in the racial politics. They are conditioned into thinking along the communal lines, but they want to break through that.”
Among the many challenges
She said one challenge for the researchers was to ensure that the findings did not simply reflect the views of the loudest or most visible members of the community.
“Being the loudest did not mean that they have a full understanding of a stipulation on ground,” she said.
Not particularly looking for a solution, Lee said the report is a qualitative research and is not statistically representative of all Malaysian Chinese youths.
“Its findings are intended to provide insight into how the participants understood their experiences, rather than measure how widespread particular views are.
“We actually only included 30 per cent of the data collected, there were just too much data which we thought was better to leave them for further research into specific communities and experiences,” she said.
For Lee, the next step is to create more opportunities for young people from different communities to speak to one another.
She said the responsibility should not fall on young people alone, but also on researchers, the media and civil society organisations to create space for discussion.
For her, the research is ultimately about giving young people more room to think about their place in the country, rather than seeing them only as voters whose views matter during elections.
“This research gets the conversation starting especially for Chinese youths who don’t know where to start, or what to do first,” she said.

Title: Anthony Loke officially resigns as transport minister following court decision on Najib
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke Siew Fook has resigned as transport minister with immediate effect following the Kuala Lumpur High Court's decision allowing former prime minister Najib Tun Razak to serve his sentence under house arrest, according to a statement issued today.
In the statement, Loke said his decision was in line with the position he had publicly stated last Friday and was based on the principles and stand he had previously outlined.
He expressed his appreciation to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim for the trust and mandate given to him to serve in the Cabinet since December 2022.
Loke also thanked the senior management and staff of the Ministry of Transport for their commitment and cooperation throughout his tenure at the ministry. He said he would provide full cooperation to ensure a smooth transition and that all ministry responsibilities and initiatives would continue to be implemented in the interest of the public.

Title: Najib to serve remaining jail term at home after High Court issues new warrant
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — The High Court has directed the Court Registrar to issue a new order that would finally allow Datuk Seri Mohd Najib Abdul Razak to serve the remaining sentence of his first corruption conviction at home.
High Court Judge Datuk Aslam Zainuddin issued the new warrant of release after hearing submissions by both Najib’s lawyers and the Deputy Public Prosecutors this afternoon.
Judge Aslam said the new order simply cancels the November 6 order and replaced with one that allows Najib to serve the remaining sentence from the said conviction at home.
“I will just read the gist of it: The order dated November 6 is hereby cancelled and is a replaced with a new order that states the defendant will serve his remaining sentence under house imprisonment,” he said.
At the hearing, Najib’s lead counsel Tan Sri Shafee Abdullah had argued that the court need not issue a new order since the first was already “very clear”.
He alleged even the Prison Department understood the discharge order, was ready to release the former prime minister but “was then told to wait”.
Shafee’s core argument was that the condition to trigger Najib’s release from Kajang Prison and serve home imprisonment - paying the RM50 million - was already met, and that the ensuing order of discharge issued by the High Court Registrar was worded in a way that reflected that.
In a press conference held shortly after the hearing ended, Shafee welcomed the clarification by Judge Aslam even has he maintained his argument that the original order was “solid in substance”, and that all matters regarding the King’s pardon need not be formalised by the judicial system.
“It is good that the court has clarified so that those who apparently found it hard to understand, will now understand,” he said.
Najib, in a light blue baju melayu top with sleeves rolled up, was present at the hearing alongside his daughter Najwa, who was also in a blue floral baju kurung.
The former prime minister was set to serve the remaining two years of his jail sentence from the corruption conviction involving SRC International arrest last Friday, after his lawyers said he had paid the RM50 million fine as part of his conditional pardon.
The AGC, however, delayed his release from Kajang Prison, claiming it needed clarification because the November 6 court order was unclear and possibly defective.
Shafee said Najib would likely be home by tonight, after all formal documents have been submitted to Kajang Prison where he would also be briefed about the conditions of his house arrest.
Details of the conditions are still not available to the lawyers for now including on visitation Shafee added.
“I assume you will have to apply, at least initially. Or they may make it easier as there is a post (at Najib’s residence), and they may device some system,” he said.
“But nevertheless, the point being you will still need to get permission.”
It is understood that Najib’s house arrest will last until August 2028.

Title: ITU PP-26: Appointment of Malaysian representative as Committee 5 chair reflects international confidence
Article:
DOHA, Nov 10 — Malaysia’s appointment as chair of Committee 5 at the 2026 International Telecommunication Union Plenipotentiary Conference (ITU PP-26) reflects the international community’s confidence in the country’s ability to play a neutral role in balancing the interests of various parties.
Committee 5 chair Eneng Faridah Iskandar said the appointment was not merely a personal recognition but a major achievement for Malaysia, according to a report published by Bernama.
“I think this is not only an achievement (but) actually an achievement for the country because Malaysia is seen as a neutral country that can accept the views of all parties.
“So, as chair, our task is to balance the interests and wishes of all parties, and we must be fair,” she told Bernama and RTM here today.
Eneng Faridah, who is also Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) Deputy Managing Director (Development), expressed her appreciation to the Malaysian government for having the confidence to nominate her for the role at the conference, which runs from November 9 to 27.
She said the position carried significant responsibility as she would not only represent Malaysia but also have to take into account the interests of all member states involved in the discussions.
Explaining Committee 5’s role, Eneng Faridah said the substantive committee was responsible for examining various policy and legal issues within the ITU framework.
More than 95 proposals covering over 40 resolutions have been submitted for discussion at this year’s conference.
“One of the main challenges is acting as an intermediary between various parties with different interests to reach a common agreement, as the ITU operates on the principle of consensus,” she said.
She said several preliminary meetings had been held ahead of the committee’s sessions, which are scheduled to begin tomorrow, to ensure that negotiations proceed smoothly.
One of the main committees at ITU PP-26, Committee 5, also known as the Policy and Legal Committee, is responsible for discussing proposed international telecommunications policies and regulations, as well as examining resolutions submitted by ITU member states.
Its chair plays a key role in conducting negotiations, balancing interests and bridging differences among member states to reach a consensus, before the committee’s deliberations are submitted to the conference for consideration and decisions.
PP-26, being held in Doha, is the ITU’s highest-level conference, convened every four years to determine the organisation’s direction, policies and strategic plans.
The Malaysian delegation to the conference is led by Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, with the mission of retaining the country’s seat on the ITU Council for the 2027-2030 term.
The ITU is a specialised agency of the United Nations (UN) responsible for information and communications technology (ICT), including setting global standards, allocating radio-frequency spectrum, coordinating satellites and efforts to bridge the global digital divide.

Title: MWC Doha: Fahmi shares Malaysia’s 5G network progress, 90pc coverage achieved ahead of schedule
Article:
DOHA, Nov 10 — Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil shared Malaysia’s progress in expanding its 5G network at Mobile World Congress (MWC) Doha 2026, with the country’s second 5G network achieving 90 per cent coverage last October, nine months ahead of schedule.
He said the achievement marked significant progress in Malaysia’s transition towards a dual 5G network model aimed at enhancing competition, encouraging investment and improving the quality of telecommunications services, according to a Bernama report.
Fahmi said Malaysia had also made substantial investments in expanding and strengthening its digital infrastructure through the National Digital Network Plan (Jendela) since 2020.
“As of July 2026, approximately 10.12 million premises had been covered by fibre-optic networks, significantly improving access to high-speed broadband services,” he said during the Ministerial Panel Forum on Digital Leadership at MWC Doha 2026 here on Sunday.
He said the developments reflected the country’s efforts to build a competitive and sustainable telecommunications ecosystem while ensuring consumers benefited from improved service quality.
However, Fahmi stressed that Malaysia’s digital infrastructure development was not solely focused on expanding network coverage, but also on service quality, subscription affordability and network resilience.
He said all these aspects needed to be addressed comprehensively to ensure digital connectivity delivered meaningful benefits to the people.
“Through the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), we continue to encourage infrastructure sharing and efficient network deployment, while addressing connectivity gaps among underserved communities,” he said.
Fahmi said the Universal Service Provision (USP) framework also played an important role in extending telecommunications services to areas that might not be commercially viable through private investment alone.
He said this approach allowed Malaysia to balance infrastructure investment with the need to ensure telecommunications services remained accessible at affordable rates.
“For Malaysia, a successful network model is one that combines strong infrastructure, sustainable investment, effective regulation and meaningful access for all,” he said.
Fahmi is in Doha to lead the Malaysian delegation to the International Telecommunication Union Plenipotentiary Conference (ITU PP-26), which runs from November 6 to 11.
His working visit also carries the important mission of securing Malaysia’s re-election to the ITU Council for the 2027-2030 term.
He is accompanied by Communications Ministry Deputy Secretary-General (Telecommunications Infrastructure) Mano Verabathran.
The Malaysian delegation also includes representatives from the MCMC and local telecommunications industry players, including Telekom Malaysia (TM), CelcomDigi, Maxis and U Mobile.

Title: Kuala Kangsar Sessions Court orders mental health assessment for accused in rape, attempted murder case
Article:
KUALA KANGSAR, Nov 10 — The Sessions Court here today ordered a man who pleaded guilty to attempting to murder and raping a woman to undergo a psychiatric assessment at Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta, Tanjung Rambutan.
Judge Nuur Hafiedzah Md Daud issued the order against Marwan Mohd Nor, 38, under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code after observing the accused’s demeanour when he pleaded guilty to both charges.
Earlier, Marwan pleaded guilty to both charges and appealed to the court to impose the maximum sentence for the rape charge.
According to the first charge, the accused was alleged to have attempted to murder a 20-year-old woman, causing her injuries by the roadside along the Felda Lasah-Lintang road, at Lubuk Kelah Lintang, Sungai Siput, at about 11.20 pm on Nov 3.
The charge was framed under Section 307(1) of the Penal Code, which provides for a jail term of up to 20 years and a possible fine upon conviction.
Under the second charge, the man was accused of causing injury to and raping the victim at the same location, date and time.
He was charged under Section 376(2)(a) of the Penal Code, which provides for a minimum jail term of 10 years and a maximum of 30 years, as well as whipping, upon conviction.
Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) prosecuting officer Insp Nor A’in Ahmad applied for a date to be fixed for the submission of the facts of the case and sentencing.
The court subsequently ordered the accused to be sent to Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta Tanjung Rambutan for monitoring and a mental health assessment, and fixed Dec 21 for mention of the case and submission of the psychiatric report. — Bernama

Title: Not cutting-edge: Men armed with scissors in Tuaran gang robbery to be sentenced on Nov 20
Article:
KOTA KINABALU, Nov 10 — Three men who pleaded guilty to a charge of gang robbery armed with scissors will know their fate on November 20.
Sessions Court Judge Monica Linsua adjourned the sentencing of the men, aged 29, 26, and 35 respectively, under Section 395 of the Penal Code, which is punishable under Section 397 of the same Code, at the request of the prosecution.
The prosecution had requested ample time to prepare the facts of the case and relevant documents before the court passed the sentence.
The men had admitted robbing another two men of their cash and two mobile phones by the roadside of Jalan Berungis in Tuaran at 12.50am on Oct 26.
The charge stated that the offence was committed with another two accomplices, who are still at large.
The offence carries a jail term of up to 20 years and caning upon conviction.
The three men were released on RM5,000 bail each with one local surety.
Monica also ordered them to report to the nearest police station once a month until the disposal of the case.
Deputy public prosecutor Fazriel Fardiansyah Abdul Kadir appeared for the prosecution, while all three men did not have legal counsel. — The Borneo Post

Title: Najib in court as lawyers, AGC discuss fresh house arrest order
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — Datuk Seri Najib Razak is present as the High Court hears the application for a new order to allow the former prime minister to serve his first jail sentence at home.
Najib, in a light blue baju melayu top with sleeves rolled up, was present at the hearing alongside his daughter Najwa, who was in a blue floral baju kurung.
The former prime minister was set to serve the remaining two years of his jail sentence from the corruption conviction involving SRC International last Friday, after his lawyers said he had paid the RM50 million fine as part of his conditional pardon.
The AGC, however, delayed his release from Kajang Prison, claiming it needed clarification because the November 6 court order was unclear and possibly defective.
The High Court is expected to issue a new warrant to release Najib from Kajang Prison this afternoon itself.

Title: Melaka polls: Pakatan takes politics to coffee shops with Gen Z-focused ‘Kopilih Harapan’ initiative
Article:
MELAKA, Nov 10 — Pakatan Harapan (PH) is adopting a new approach to engage young people, particularly Generation Z, through its ‘Kopilih Harapan’ programme, which provides an informal platform for political leaders and members of the public to discuss current issues and aspirations.
PH Election Department (JPPH) Media Unit head Jonathan Vela said the programme aims to foster more open and inclusive two-way communication, moving away from conventional political ceramah.
He said the coffee shop-themed initiative allows young people to raise questions, share their views and seek clarification directly from PH leaders and candidates.
“We want to provide them with a platform to discuss and exchange views, rather than simply listen to political speeches. It also gives them an opportunity to get to know their leaders and understand politics better,” he told a press conference at the PH Main Operations Room in Bukit Piatu here today.
Jonathan said the programme would feature Lembah Jaya assemblyman Syed Ahmad Syed Abdul Rahman Al-Hadad, better known as Altimet, Bentong Member of Parliament Young Syefura Othman, Hang Tuah Jaya MP Adam Adli Abd Halim and several other PH leaders.
He said Kopilih Harapan would visit several locations frequented by young people across the state during the 16th Melaka state election campaign, in collaboration with local coffee shops, while also supporting small-scale entrepreneurs and the local coffee industry.
Meanwhile, Altimet, who is also the Kopilih Harapan ambassador, said the initiative took into account changing media consumption habits among younger generations, who were increasingly accustomed to interactive communication rather than one-way information delivery.
“Based on my experience, engaging with them through a forum that is not in the form of a political speech but rather a dialogue session is more effective.
“We also give them the opportunity to decide what they want to discuss. When we share the direction of the session with them, young people feel that they are part of the programme,” said the former rapper.
Altimet said the approach should be expanded beyond PH, including among Members of Parliament and state assemblymen, to engage the public, particularly young voters.
Polling is set for Nov 14. For the latest updates on the 16th Melaka state election, visit
https://election.bernama.com/prn/melaka/2026/
. — Bernama

Title: Skilled workforce crucial to unlocking Malaysia’s high-tech investment potential, says minister
Article:
PETALING JAYA, Nov 10 — Developing a highly skilled workforce must remain a priority for Malaysia to fully capitalise on opportunities arising from digital transformation and the rapid growth of high-tech industries.
Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Datuk Chang Lih Kang said that while Malaysia continues to attract billions of ringgit in high-tech sector investments, the country’s success ultimately depends on its local workforce’s ability to master and harness emerging technologies.
“Malaysia is currently at the forefront of the regional digital transformation, with global companies choosing the country as an investment destination for artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductor manufacturing, smart factories and renewable energy, further strengthening our position as the digital backbone of the Asia-Pacific region.
“However, behind these investments lies a fundamental truth: machines do not build nations, people do,” he said at the official opening of Schneider Electric’s Regional Training Center (RTC) here today.
Chang said the rapid adoption of digitalisation, advanced automation and complex electrification had increased demand for workers with technical expertise and skills aligned with industry requirements.
“Without equipping our engineers, technicians and young Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) talents with practical, industry-relevant skills, we risk leaving our workforce behind as technology continues to advance,” he added.
He said initiatives such as Schneider Electric’s RTC were important in bridging the gap between academic education and industry requirements while preparing Malaysians for opportunities in the growing digital economy.
Chang said industry investments in human capital development also reinforced the principle that Malaysia’s greatest asset was its people, ensuring national innovation policies translated into tangible economic outcomes.
He also highlighted Malaysia’s achievement in securing 34th place out of 139 economies in the 2026 Global Innovation Index.
Malaysia recorded more than RM200 billion in approved investments in the first half of this year, including RM95 billion in data centres and cloud infrastructure, particularly in Selangor and Johor.
The 18,500-square-foot facility can train more than 550 participants annually from 15 Asia-Pacific countries through hands-on technical exercises using operational equipment and real-world industry scenarios.
Chang officiated the opening ceremony. Also present were French Ambassador to Malaysia Marc Abensour, Malaysian French Chamber of Commerce and Industry president Richard Fostier and Schneider Electric Malaysia country president Eugene Quah.
The event also coincides with Schneider Electric’s 40th anniversary in Malaysia, marking four decades of the company’s contribution to the country’s industrial development, energy transition and technological advancement. — Bernama
